parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *dragɔ̄n, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *dragōnis, from Latin dracō, dracōnem, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn).
From an earlier kūt, from Proto-Albanian *kuβət, borrowed via Vulgar Latin from Latin cubitum (“elbow, cubit”). Compare also Aromanian, Romanian cot.
From Proto-Albanian *kambjɔnit (> third person singular këmben), borrowed from Vulgar Latin *cambiō, from Late Latin cambīre, from Latin cambium, from Gaulish cambion.
From an earlier mjēk, from Proto-Albanian *mʲeðək, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin medicus (“doctor, physician, surgeon”).

Demiraj claims descent from Proto-Albanian *m(i)ier-, cognate to Ancient Greek μιερός (mierós), μιαρός (miarós, “polluted, defiled”). On the other hand, Orel claims a borrowing through Vulgar Latin from Latin miser, although this does not reflect the phonetics of Latin loanwords into Albanian.

From Old Albanian mpson (Bogdani, Budi), ëmpson (Buzuku), from Proto-Albanian *imbitjɔnit, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *invitiō, *invitiāre, from *vitiō, from Latin vitium (“vice”). Compare Romanian învăța. Otherwise from pësoj, itself of Latin origin, developing in mpsoj, psoj, mbsoj, mbësoj and oth
From earlier pëlqenj (third person singular pëlqen), from Proto-Albanian *plakjɔnit, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin placeō. Compare Romanian plăcea, Italian piacere.
From earlier pësonj (third person singular pëson), from Proto-Albanian *patjɔnit, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *patīre from Latin patī (“suffer”). Compare Romanian păți, Italian patire.

parole.significato: city, particularly (politics, historical) as a former administrative level
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Albanian *k'iwytéti, from older *kiwitáti, which was borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cīvitātem, with loss of the -v-. Compare Romanian cetate.
From an earlier shërbenj (third person singular shërben), from Proto-Albanian *śerbi̯ɔnit, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *serbiō, from Latin serviō.
From Proto-Albanian *u̯ɔλa, from Vulgar Latin *oli̯u, from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).
From Proto-Albanian *u̯œrbana-, borrowed from Vulgar Latin ōrbus, from Latin orbus (“deprived”). compare Italian orbo, Dalmatian vuarb, Romanian orb.
